summary: Specifies BRSKI, an automated process for securely bootstrapping a new device into a network. It uses manufacturer-installed X.509 certificates together with a manufacturer's authorizing service, which can be online or offline, to set up a key infrastructure without manual configuration.

eli5.summary: A brand-new device shows an ID from its maker, the network checks it, and the device is trusted without anyone typing in secrets.

questions: how to securely onboard a new network device
how does a pledge get a voucher
what is a masa in brski
subtitle: How a brand-new device proves who it is, learns who owns the network, and joins with no manual setup.

tldr.problem: A new, unconfigured device and the network it joins do not yet trust each other, and the usual fixes are touch-based, costly pre-provisioning, or insecure trust on first use.
tldr.mechanism: The device presents a factory-installed IDevID certificate. The domain registrar asks the manufacturer's MASA service for a signed voucher naming the registrar as the owner, and the device accepts the registrar only if it can verify that voucher.
tldr.outcome: The device ends up with a trust anchor for its domain and a TLS connection usable for EST enrollment, with an audit-log for the registrar to inspect. The price is reliance on the manufacturer and some privacy exposure.

today: RFC 8995 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 8366 for the voucher format and on RFC 7030 for enrollment.

sections.title: The Bootstrapping Problem
sections.content:
BRSKI (Bootstrapping Remote Secure Key Infrastructure) is a protocol for secure zero-touch bootstrap of new, unconfigured devices called pledges. Each pledge has an IDevID (Initial Device Identifier), an X.509 certificate installed at the factory. The abstract notes that the process can work with a routable address and a cloud service, with only link-local connectivity, or in limited or disconnected networks.

Before anything else, the pledge and the domain's registrar must settle four questions: the registrar authenticates and authorizes the pledge, and the pledge authenticates and authorizes the registrar. The IDevID and a TLS connection answer the first two. A signed artifact called a voucher, issued by the manufacturer's service, answers the other two.

The RFC contrasts this with earlier approaches: trust on first use, pre-shared keys loaded on each device, or EST's manual step of having a person authorize the CA certificate. 'Call home' designs require real-time contact with the manufacturer, expose the domain's identity to it, and make it responsible for authorization decisions. BRSKI primarily serves the Autonomic Control Plane of RFC 8994, and is aimed at non-constrained devices, not constrained 802.15.4 low-power networks.
sections.eli5: A new toy has to find out who its owner is, but anyone could claim to be the owner. The toy's maker writes a signed note naming the real one, and the toy checks the maker's signature.

sections.title: The Cast of Characters
sections.content:
The architecture has these parts.

  • Pledge: the new device, assumed to talk to the proxy over link-local connectivity.
  • Join Proxy: gives limited HTTPS connectivity between pledge and registrar. The defined form is a stateful circuit proxy that passes TLS bytes through without examining them.
  • Domain Registrar: authenticates the pledge, decides whether to accept it, and gets vouchers from the manufacturer service. It may also act as a PKI registration authority.
  • Manufacturer service (MASA): the Manufacturer Authorized Signing Authority signs vouchers and keeps an audit-log. An optional ownership tracker can record who bought which device.
  • PKI: issues the domain's certificates.

The IDevID is a certificate with no common root required; each manufacturer can make its own. The RFC defines a non-critical certificate extension that carries the MASA URI, which is normally reduced to an authority, with https:// and /.well-known/brski assumed. Devices that lack a clock may ignore certificate and voucher times, and long-lived IDevID certificates SHOULD use the notAfter value 99991231235959Z.
sections.eli5: There is the new gadget, a helper at the door, the building manager who decides who gets in, and the gadget's maker who signs a note about the manager. A record keeper writes down every note.

sections.title: The Protocol Flow
sections.content:
A pledge goes through five states: discover a channel to a registrar, identify itself with its IDevID in a TLS handshake (accepting the registrar's certificate only provisionally), request to join with a unique nonce, imprint on the registrar by verifying a voucher, and enroll. It returns to discovery if it is rejected, gets a bad MASA response, fails to enroll, or is factory reset.

The registrar checks the pledge's request, then forwards the information, including the pledge's serial number, to the MASA over TLS. The MASA applies its policy and may issue a voucher. The voucher goes to the registrar first, not straight to the device, so the registrar can examine the voucher and the MASA's audit-logs. The registrar then passes it on, and the pledge sends status telemetry. EST enrollment can follow on the now bidirectionally authenticated TLS session.

The pledge's request is an HTTPS POST to /.well-known/brski/requestvoucher. The pledge MUST sign it with its IDevID, include a strong random nonce that differs for every attempt, set assertion to proximity, and include the registrar's TLS certificate as proximity-registrar-cert. The registrar builds its own signed voucher-request for the MASA, copying the nonce and attaching the pledge's request as prior-signed-voucher-request. It MUST read the serial number from the pledge's certificate and not simply copy the claimed one.
sections.eli5: The gadget asks for help, the manager asks the maker 'is this really mine?', and the maker's signed reply comes back to the manager first. The manager checks it and hands it to the gadget.

sections.title: The Voucher-Request
sections.content:
The voucher-request is a minor extension of the voucher format in RFC 8366, defined in a YANG module. Its leaves include created-on, expires-on, assertion, serial-number, idevid-issuer, pinned-domain-cert, nonce, prior-signed-voucher-request and proximity-registrar-cert.

The pledge signs a pledge voucher-request with its IDevID, and the registrar signs a registrar voucher-request with its own key. The proximity assertion in the ACP context rests on the pledge being at most one IPv6 link-local hop from an ACP node. A registrar can also send a nonceless request, with no prior-signed request, to get a voucher for later offline use, for example when it cannot reach the MASA during deployment. It needs to learn the serial number out of band, such as from a bar code or the sales channel.
sections.eli5: The request is a form with the gadget's serial number, a one-time secret number and a copy of the manager's badge. It is signed so nobody can forge it.

sections.title: Finding a Proxy and Registrar
sections.content:
In the ACP, the pledge gets an IPv6 address and listens for GRASP M_FLOOD announcements of the objective AN_Proxy, which proxies send to announce themselves. Other methods such as mDNS are active and run in parallel; they SHOULD back off by doubling to a maximum of one hour.

A pledge SHOULD try every discovered proxy until a valid voucher arrives, in parallel so a slow fake proxy cannot stall it, with attempts to different proxies sent at intervals of 3 to 5s. Each attempt through a distinct proxy MUST use a unique nonce. The proxy learns about registrars through AN_join_registrar announcements, which MUST be sent periodically; the default period SHOULD be 60 seconds. TCP proxying is mandatory, and other methods are optional.

Without a local registrar, a pledge MAY contact a well-known URI of a cloud registrar, authenticated using a manufacturer-assigned trust anchor database.
sections.eli5: The helper at the door keeps shouting 'I can take you inside!' The new gadget listens, and tries each helper it hears.

sections.title: Checking the Voucher
sections.content:
The pledge-registrar connection uses TLS, with TLS 1.2 or newer REQUIRED on the pledge. Until the voucher is verified, the connection is provisional: the pledge could be talking to an attacker, so it MUST treat all received data, including HTTP headers and the CMS voucher, as untrusted.

When the voucher arrives, the pledge MUST verify its signature using the manufacturer-installed trust anchors, check that the serial number matches its own, and check the nonce if present. It then treats the public key in the voucher's pinned-domain-cert as the sole temporary trust anchor and validates the registrar's TLS certificate chain against it. If that fails, the pledge discards the connection and tries other proxies. If it succeeds, the connection is no longer provisional.

The MASA checks the registrar's request too. It confirms the signer's certificate has the id-kp-cmcRA extended key usage, and if a prior-signed request is present, that its proximity certificate and nonce match. A registrar MAY reply 202 with a retry time; the pledge MUST limit it to 60 seconds, SHOULD tolerate retry state for up to 4 days, and MUST resend the same request. The RFC recommends a voucher lifetime on the order of 20 minutes.
sections.eli5: The gadget checks the maker's signature, its own serial number and the secret number. Only then does it decide the manager is the real owner.

sections.title: Telemetry, Audit-Logs and Enrollment
sections.content:
After processing the voucher, the pledge MUST report status to the registrar with a POST to .well-known/brski/voucher_status. The JSON has a version and a boolean status, and a reason when the status is false. The reason SHOULD NOT help an attacker, since the registrar may be malicious.

The registrar SHOULD then request the device's audit-log from the MASA. Entries hold a date, a domainID identifying the earlier registrar, the nonce (or null), and an assertion of verified, logged or proximity. The registrar uses these to detect surprises, such as a supposedly new device with prior owners, or nonceless entries that would let an earlier owner take over after a reset. If its policy is violated it can revoke credentials or refuse the voucher, and it MUST then refuse any EST actions.

Afterward the pledge SHOULD run EST enrollment over the same connection, fetching CA certificates and CSR attributes and requesting a certificate (a locally issued LDevID). Enrolled devices SHOULD announce themselves as Join Proxies to help later devices.
sections.eli5: The gadget tells the manager how it went. The manager reads the record of previous owners the maker kept and can say no if anything looks odd.

sections.title: Reduced Security Modes, Privacy and Risks
sections.content:
The RFC describes optional lower-security modes as informative guidance that profiles must specify. A pledge MUST accept nonceless vouchers and MUST NOT support trust on first use on network interfaces, though it MAY have a one-time mechanism to skip voucher validation, such as via a console. A registrar MAY accept any device or unauthenticated entities, but these MUST NOT be defaults. A MASA may issue long-lived nonceless vouchers or skip ownership checks, relying on the audit-log as defense in depth.

Privacy costs are real. The MASA audit-log contains domain identities, and the MASA learns about deployed devices; the RFC has sections on resale, stolen and grey market equipment, and the death of a manufacturer. A key point is that BRSKI does not change the underlying trust in the manufacturer: the domain still has to trust it, and a compromised MASA signing key or IDevID signing key is a serious risk.

Other security points: the MASA can be a DoS target, so registrars can keep long-term nonceless vouchers. The domainID needs a hash resistant to second-preimage attacks, and the nonce needs good randomness. A fake registrar that collects a voucher is caught by the real registrar checking the audit-log.
sections.eli5: There are back doors for emergencies, but they are never the default. And you have to trust the maker, because its signed note is what everything depends on.

viz.caption: HTTP RESPONSES IN THE VOUCHER EXCHANGE

items.label: OK
items.desc: Successful request; the voucher is returned.

items.label: Accepted
items.desc: Not yet processed; the pledge waits for the retry time, capped at 60 seconds.

items.label: Forbidden
items.desc: Request not signed correctly, stale, or the pledge has another outstanding voucher.

items.label: Not Found
items.desc: Device unknown to the MASA, or validation failed at the registrar.

items.label: Not Acceptable
items.desc: A voucher of the desired type cannot be issued, or the registrar rejects the pledge.

items.label: Unsupported Media Type
items.desc: Voucher-request or Accept value not understood.
